title: Hosting unit price sensitivity - Pegasus Retail intake
summary: Discovery focused on per-token pricing sensitivity and tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Customer runs high-volume product search and personalization models; primary constraints: strict budget cap, SLOs for p99 latency, and data residency. Discussed batching, prefix/KV cache, quantization, routing/fallbacks, and pilot scope. Agreed next steps: pricing worksheet, security docs, and a pilot run with sample traffic for unit-econ modelling.
questions: Can Redwood guarantee p99 under 200ms for our 512-token median request?
What are expected cost savings from KV prefix caching for our traffic mix?
How does dedicated pricing change with reserved commit vs burst capacity?
next_steps: Redwood: send pricing worksheet and pilot SOW (Maya)
Redwood: share SOC2 and VPC security brief (Luis)
Customer: provide sample token histogram + 7 days of anonymized request traces (Sarah)
Schedule technical pilot kickoff next week (tentative)
action_items: Maya - Email pricing worksheet and sample pilot SOW by 2025-10-13
Luis - Attach SOC 2 excerpt and VPC/KMS notes by 2025-10-11
Sarah - Share anonymized request traces and token histogram by 2025-10-14
transcript: Meeting header: Date: 2025-10-09 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Hannah Park (Redwood CSM); Sarah Patel (Pegasus Head of ML), Tom Hughes (CTO), Priya Raman (Infra)
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Sarah: Hi, Sarah here.
[00:10] Tom: Tom, hi.
[00:12] Priya: Priya on infra. Morning all.
[00:15] Luis: Luis from Redwood, I'll be the technical lead here.

[00:19] Maya: Cool, thanks. Goal for today is to understand Pegasus's cost constraints and see which hosting mode fits — hosted, dedicated, or private — and what levers move the per-token price. We'll talk batching, KV/prefix cache, quantization, and routing/fallbacks. Sound good?

[00:36] Tom: Yep, that's right. Budget is the hard constraint — we have a monthly cap and we can't overshoot. Also need p99 latency under ~200ms for personalization calls, and data residency in the EU for payment-related fields.

[00:52] Sarah: To add: our model is a 7B-ish transformer for ranking+rerank, median request length ~120 tokens but 95th around 600 when we include context. We do a lot of batched requests from frontend — sometimes micro-batches from edge — and also heavy session caching for logged-in customers.
[01:15] Luis: Useful. So you have a heavy tail. That matters for batching/throughput. Couple clarifying Qs: are you okay with slight quality delta from int8/4-bit quantization if it halves GPU cost?
[01:29] Sarah: Maybe. We need an A/B with our human evals. If quality loss is negligible, sure. But can't be a regression on NDCG for search results.

[01:38] Maya: On pricing: Redwood hosted per-token is usage-based; dedicated moves you to reserved commits with lower per-token but fixed monthly. Private has platform fees plus infra. Luis, can you give quick knobs?

[01:49] Luis: Yeah — main levers: batching (amortize kernel startup), continuous KV/prefix cache (avoid re-computation for repeated prefixes), quantization (lower GPU mem and more instances per GPU), and smart routing (send low-SLO traffic to cheaper variants). For Pegasus traffic — with lots of repeated context — prefix caching could be substantial. Ballpark: caching could cut token compute by 20-45% depending on hit rate. Batching depends on tail; average throughput improvement maybe 1.5-2x if you can accept 20-40ms added latency in some cases.
[02:28] Tom: That 20-45% is a big range. What inputs does that depend on?

[02:33] Luis: Primarily cache hit rate (how often prefixes repeat), the average prefix length we can reuse, and whether the application is tolerant to slightly stale cached KVs for session embeddings. Also model architecture; some models cache more efficiently.
[02:50] Priya: We can run a sample to estimate hit rate. We'll need to sanitize logs though. Any concerns with data residency if we share anonymized traces?
[02:58] Maya: We can accept anonymized traces. We'll sign an NDA and you can obfuscate tokens. For the SOW we'll list data handling constraints. Luis — note SOC2/ISO and VPC options here.

[03:12] Luis: Yep, Redwood offers hosted with EU-region tenancy, Dedicated with reserved pools in EU, and Private (VPC or on-prem). For Private we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. I'll attach our compliance pack.
[03:25] Sarah: Good. On the pricing model itself — do you do separate per-embedding and per-token pricing? We have both embedding workloads and generative reranking, so we care across both.

[03:33] Maya: Yes, embeddings are separate units — typically cheaper per call but throughput patterns differ. We'll map both in the pricing worksheet. For tokens, we price input+output tokens. For embeddings it's per-vector unit.
[03:45] Tom: Walk me through an example: suppose we have 10 million tokens per day, median 120 tokens — what's rough monthly cost hosted vs dedicated?

[03:56] Luis: Off the cuff: hosted per-token rates are higher but flexible — for 10M/day you could run into cost where dedicated reserved capacity with a commit could be 20-40% cheaper depending on commitment length and instance types. But exact depends on burst patterns and SLOs. We'll run models against your traces to produce a unit-econ table.
[04:20] Sarah: We need to capture the hidden costs — egress, long-tail latency penalties, and guardrails. How does Redwood handle overflow/burst?

[04:31] Maya: We have configurable burst capacity for Dedicated and hosted fallback. When you're at commit limits we can route to lower-cost model variants or throttle — policy-controlled. Also can use multi-tier routing: premium pool for low-latency calls, bulk pool for less sensitive.
[04:46] Priya: Are fallbacks automatic? I don't want sudden model regressions affecting customers.

[04:51] Luis: Fallbacks are policy-led and you define acceptable variants. We recommend canarying variants and having automatic rollback on quality regressions. For high SLO calls, keep a warm pool of identical model variants.
[05:05] Tom: About quantization: what is the recommended path? We're worried about dev ops complexity if we need special kernels or runtime hacks.

[05:15] Luis: Redwood handles quantization execution paths in the runtime — you pick quantization profile and we handle kernel selection. Some models require tuned kernels; we manage that and surface tradeoffs in the console. Ops work is minimal for hosted/dedicated; Private may need more tuning onsite.
[05:30] Sarah: That helps. For pilot scope, we want a 2-week run against sample traffic to estimate p99 and unit costs. Can Redwood simulate prefix caching improvements?

[05:39] Luis: Yes, we run a trace-based simulator that can estimate caching hit rates and batching impact. It models sequence length distribution and routing policies. It's accurate within ~10-15% historically.
[05:54] Hannah: I'll coordinate the pilot SOW items. We'll need: sanitized traces, target SLOs, traffic windows, and expected KPIs (cost per 1k tokens, p50/p95/p99 latency).
[06:07] Sarah: We'll aim to provide 7 days of traces and a token histogram. Timeline: can we start next week?
[06:12] Maya: Yes, next week kickoff is possible. We'll prepare the pricing worksheet and a draft SOW first.
[06:18] Tom: One more: data residency; for EU-only traffic we need no US egress at any time and audit logs. Private seemed appealing for this — but cost is a concern. How much premium is private?

[06:28] Luis: Private has platform licensing and support fees on top of infra costs. For EU-only it's often 1.4-1.8x hosted in initial year depending on on-prem vs VPC. But Private gives more control for KMS and network egress. Dedicated in EU is a middle ground — lower per-token than hosted, with VPC options and audit logs.
[06:46] Priya: We also have strict SSO requirements (SAML/Okta) and role-based access. Does Redwood support RBAC and audit trails?
[06:54] Maya: Yes, RBAC, SAML SSO, and audit logs are available on enterprise tiers. We'll include the exact feature mapping in the security brief.
[07:02] Sarah: Back to unit economics: show me a scenario table where caching hit rate is low vs high. I want to see the delta on monthly spend and required commits for dedicated.

[07:12] Luis: We'll prepare a three-scenario table: pessimistic (5% cache hit), realistic (25%), optimistic (55%). For each scenario we'll show tokens saved, estimated GPU hours, and per-token effective cost across hosting modes.
[07:26] Tom: Perfect. Also include sensitivity to batch window: if we increase latency allowance by 30ms, what's the batching win?
[07:33] Luis: We'll model that too — batching window sensitivity for median vs peak.
[07:38] Priya: Operationally, if we do Dedicated reserved commit, how does autoscaling behave during holiday traffic spikes?

[07:45] Luis: Dedicated supports autoscaling and burst capacity. You define a baseline reserved commit and then set a burst budget; billing for burst is usage-based. We'll show a projection for holiday spikes vs baseline.
[07:58] Sarah: Any gotchas around token counting? Sometimes we see different vendor counts depending on whitespace/tokenizer differences.
[08:06] Luis: Yup, tokenizer differences matter. We'll normalize by running your tokenizer in our sim. Also need to confirm whether system prompts are included in counting for your metrics.

[08:17] Maya: Quick pause — does anyone have strong objections to hosted trial first? It tends to be fastest to iterate on econ. If budget is the biggest limiter, you could pilot hosted and then map to dedicated if it makes sense.
[08:28] Tom: Hosted trial is fine, as long as EU residency is respected and we have audit logs. If we see unexpected burn we can switch to dedicate commit conversation.
[08:38] Sarah: One more question: competitor mentioned ModelCloud — they claim better sustained throughput for 7B with lower burn. How does Redwood compare?

[08:47] Luis: Performance differs by runtime optimizations; Redwood focuses on kernel selection and KV cache to improve sustained throughput. We'll provide benchmark artifacts. Historically our cost/Tk is comparable or better when caching and batching opportunities exist.
[08:59] Maya: We'll include benchmarking notes and raw numbers in the follow-up.

[09:03] Hannah: OK, last bit on next steps and owners. We captured actions — Maya will send pricing, Luis security docs, Sarah will send traces. Timeline: pricing + SOW by Oct 13, docs by Oct 11, traces by Oct 14. Pilot kickoff week of Oct 20 — tentative.
[09:22] Tom: That timeline works for us. Any blockers on Redwood side?
[09:27] Luis: Need the sanitized traces and confirmation of region/EU residency. Also clarify which endpoints are high-priority (personalization vs batch re-rank).
[09:38] Priya: We'll mark personalization p99 as critical and embeddings as lower priority.
[09:45] Sarah: Quick note: we expect seasonal holiday spike modeling — include a 3x traffic stress test in pilot run.
[09:53] Luis: Noted, we'll include stress-run plan.
[10:00] Maya: Any final questions?
[10:03] Tom: None from me.
[10:05] Sarah: All good.
[10:08] Maya: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the sheet and SOW. Talk soon.
[10:12] End of meeting
